question: The World Health Organization (WHO) has long been more influenced by politics than by public health, especially when faced with attempts by authoritarian regimes to use their power to shape its decisions and obstruct independent scientific investigations. The WHO has been heavily criticised for its handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, even to the point of being accused of indirectly contributing to its spread.

The organisation allegedly relied on what the Chinese Communist Party said, even with regard to the origins of the virus. Since then, there have been no reforms to the WHO’s governance, financial and budgetary management processes or arrangements concerning the transparency of its public or private funders. In view of the above: 1.
What has the Commission done to support the reform of the WHO, including with regard to the International Health Regulations (IHR) and the new pandemic treaty (WHO CA +)?
In light of the possible upcoming reforms, how does it think that the WHO could exchange information without infringing upon the sovereignty of the Member States?
Does it think there are risks to the integrity of EU citizens’ health data and what guarantees does the WHO provide to safeguard their health data?
answer: The Commission sees the intergovernmental negotiations of the Pandemic Agreement and the amendments to the International Health Regulations (IHR) as an important opportunity to address gaps exposed by the COVID-19 pandemic. The objective of the negotiations is to strengthen national, regional and global capacities for the prevention, preparedness for and response to public health emergencies.

No proposal under negotiations is intended to transfer sovereignty to the World Health Organisation (WHO). The principle of sovereignty stands as one of the guiding principles in the proposal for negotiating the text of the Pandemic Agreemen t (1), and it is clearly laid out in the IHR (2). Powers of the WHO are strictly defined in its Constitution, which is a legally binding international agreement.
In line with its Constitution, WHO cannot impose binding measures on countries, and this will not be modified by the ongoing negotiations.

As with all international agreements, any binding commitments which may be established under the Pandemic Agreement or the amended IHR would be agreed by Member States and by the Regional Economic Integration Organisations participating in the negotiations considering their domestic laws.

The EU, represented by the Commission in accordance with the authorisation to negotiate given by the Council of the European Union, and assisted by its Member States, is actively participating throughout both negotiations, with textual suggestions for concrete and practical provisions (3).
The Commission, as the EU negotiator, is also watchful to ensure that the final texts are in line with EU policies and laws, including those on privacy and data protection requirements.
